Calculus · Part V · Several variables

Module 18Optimisation in several variables

Find the highest and lowest points of a function of two or more variables. You will classify critical points with the Hessian, find absolute extreme values on closed bounded regions, optimise under constraints with Lagrange multipliers, fit a line to data by least squares, and see why gradient descent can zigzag when a function curves much more steeply in one direction than in another.

⏱ 270 minYou need: Module 8 (optimisation in one variable) and Modules 16 and 17 (vectors, partial derivatives and the gradient); the quadratic approximation uses Taylor polynomials from Module 15, and one optional proof uses Taylor’s theorem from the same module

In this module you will

  • Find the critical points of a function of two variables and classify them with the second derivative test
  • Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of a continuous function on a closed bounded region
  • Solve optimisation problems with constraints by Lagrange multipliers, and explain the method with level curves
  • Fit a line to data by least squares, deriving the normal equations from partial derivatives
  • Explain how the step size and the shape of the level curves decide whether, and how fast, gradient descent converges
1

Local extrema and critical points

Picture a function of two variables as a landscape: above the point (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) of a map the ground is at height z=f(x,y),z = f(x, y)\mathclose{\text{,}}z=f(x,y), and the level curves f(x,y)=cf(x, y) = cf(x,y)=c are the contour lines of the map (Module 17). Three kinds of place have level ground underfoot: the top of a hill, the bottom of a hollow, and a mountain pass, the lowest point of a ridge and the highest point of the path across it. This module finds such places and tells them apart. Then it finds the extreme values of a function on a region, optimises under constraints, fits lines to data, and studies how gradient descent, a method used to train machine-learning models, searches for the bottom of a valley. Unless a passage says otherwise, fff is a function of two variables; most of the ideas extend to more.

Definition 18.1Local and absolute extrema

Let fff be a function of two variables with domain D,D\mathclose{\text{,}}D, and let (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) be a point of D.D\mathclose{\text{.}}D.

  • f(a,b)f(a, b)f(a,b) is the absolute maximum value of fff if f(a,b)≥f(x,y)f(a, b) \ge f(x, y)f(a,b)≥f(x,y) for every point (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) of D,D\mathclose{\text{,}}D, and the absolute minimum value if f(a,b)≤f(x,y)f(a, b) \le f(x, y)f(a,b)≤f(x,y) for every (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) in D.D\mathclose{\text{.}}D.
  • f(a,b)f(a, b)f(a,b) is a local maximum value of fff if f(a,b)≥f(x,y)f(a, b) \ge f(x, y)f(a,b)≥f(x,y) for every (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) in some open disc centred at (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) that lies in D,D\mathclose{\text{,}}D, and a local minimum value if f(a,b)≤f(x,y)f(a, b) \le f(x, y)f(a,b)≤f(x,y) for every (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) in such a disc.

The open disc of radius r>0r > 0r>0 centred at (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) is the set of points (x,y)(x, y)(x,y) with (x−a)2+(y−b)2<r2:(x - a)^2 + (y - b)^2 < r^2\mathclose{\text{:}}(x−a)2+(y−b)2<r2: the points whose distance from (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) is less than r.r\mathclose{\text{.}}r.

These are the extreme values, or extrema. “Local” means “compared with every nearby point, in every direction”, so a point on the edge of the domain is never a local extremum, as in Module 8.

If fff has a local maximum or a local minimum at (a,b),(a, b)\mathclose{\text{,}}(a,b), and the first partial derivatives of fff exist at (a,b),(a, b)\mathclose{\text{,}}(a,b), then

fx(a,b)=0andfy(a,b)=0,f_x(a, b) = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad f_y(a, b) = 0,fx​(a,b)=0andfy​(a,b)=0,

Definition 18.2Critical point

A critical point of fff is a point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) of its domain where ∇f(a,b)=0,\nabla f(a, b) = \vb{0}\mathclose{\text{,}}∇f(a,b)=0, that is, fx(a,b)=fy(a,b)=0,f_x(a, b) = f_y(a, b) = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}fx​(a,b)=fy​(a,b)=0, or where fxf_xfx​ or fyf_yfy​ does not exist.

In these words, Theorem 18.1 says: every local extremum is at a critical point. As in one variable, the converse fails. The simplest example is f(x,y)=x2−y2.f(x, y) = x^2 - y^2\mathclose{\text{.}}f(x,y)=x2−y2. Its gradient ∇f=⟨2x,−2y⟩\nabla f = \langle 2x, -2y\rangle∇f=⟨2x,−2y⟩ is 0\vb{0}0 only at the origin, where f(0,0)=0.f(0, 0) = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}f(0,0)=0. Definition 18.3Saddle point

A critical point (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) in the interior of the domain of fff (so some open disc centred there lies in the domain) is a saddle point if fff has neither a local maximum nor a local minimum there: every open disc centred at (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) contains domain points where f(x,y)>f(a,b)f(x, y) > f(a, b)f(x,y)>f(a,b) and points where f(x,y)<f(a,b).f(x, y) < f(a, b)\mathclose{\text{.}}f(x,y)<f(a,b).

Common contour pictures are small closed loops around a hilltop or a hollow, and a level curve crossing itself at a saddle point, like the lines y=±xy = \pm xy=±x in Figure 18.1. These pictures are guides, not definitions: a saddle’s level curve need not cross itself, as x2+y3=0x^2 + y^3 = 0x2+y3=0 in Example 18.3 will show.

The second derivative test

Module 8 told a peak from a valley by the sign of f′′(c).f''(c)\mathclose{\text{.}}f′′(c). In two variables the test uses all three second partial derivatives, and the reason is a quadratic approximation.

Definition 18.4The Hessian and its determinant

The Hessian matrix of fff at (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) is the square array of its second partial derivatives there,

H=(fxxfxyfyxfyy),H = \begin{pmatrix} f_{xx} & f_{xy} \\ f_{yx} & f_{yy} \end{pmatrix},H=(fxx​fyx​​fxy​fyy​​),

and, when fyx=fxy,f_{yx} = f_{xy}\mathclose{\text{,}}fyx​=fxy​, its determinant is the number

D=fxxfyy−fxy2.D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2.D=fxx​fyy​−fxy2​.

(A rectangular array of numbers is a matrix; the determinant of a two-by-two matrix (pqrs)\begin{pmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{pmatrix}(pr​qs​) is ps−qr.)ps - qr\mathclose{\text{.)}}ps−qr.)

DDD is the AC−B2AC - B^2AC−B2 of the completed square. Mathematical Foundations studies matrices in its linear algebra modules, and in its Module 13 the quadratic forms behind this test in any number of variables.

Theorem 18.2The second derivative test

Suppose that the second partial derivatives of fff are continuous on an open disc centred at (a,b),(a, b)\mathclose{\text{,}}(a,b), and that fx(a,b)=0f_x(a, b) = 0fx​(a,b)=0 and fy(a,b)=0.f_y(a, b) = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}fy​(a,b)=0. Let D=fxx(a,b)fyy(a,b)−fxy(a,b)2.D = f_{xx}(a, b)f_{yy}(a, b) - f_{xy}(a, b)^2\mathclose{\text{.}}D=fxx​(a,b)fyy​(a,b)−fxy​(a,b)2.

  • If D>0D > 0D>0 and fxx(a,b)>0,f_{xx}(a, b) > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}fxx​(a,b)>0, then f(a,b)f(a, b)f(a,b) is a local minimum value.
  • If D>0D > 0D>0 and fxx(a,b)<0,f_{xx}(a, b) < 0\mathclose{\text{,}}fxx​(a,b)<0, then f(a,b)f(a, b)f(a,b) is a local maximum value.

When D>0,D > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}D>0, fxxfyy>fxy2≥0,f_{xx}f_{yy} > f_{xy}^2 \ge 0\mathclose{\text{,}}fxx​fyy​>fxy2​≥0, so fxxf_{xx}fxx​ and fyyf_{yy}fyy​ have the same sign, and either one decides. The continuity of the second partial derivatives is what makes the quadratic QQQ describe fff near (a,b);(a, b)\mathclose{\text{;}}(a,b); the proof below shows where it is used.

Compute itClassifying critical points with SymPy

sp.hessian builds the Hessian matrix, and solve with a list of equations solves the system ∇f=0.\nabla f = \vb{0}\mathclose{\text{.}}∇f=0. Declare the symbols real, so that only real solutions come back:

Python
import sympy as sp
x, y = sp.symbols('x y', real=True)
f = x**3 + y**3 - 3*x*y
crit = sp.solve([sp.diff(f, x), sp.diff(f, y)], [x, y], dict=True)
H = sp.hessian(f, (x, y))
print(crit)
print(H, ' D =', H.det())
Output
[{x: 0, y: 0}, {x: 1, y: 1}]
Matrix([[6*x, -3], [-3, 6*y]])  D = 36*x*y - 9

The test itself is three comparisons:

Python
def classify(D, fxx):
    if D > 0:
        return 'local minimum' if fxx > 0 else 'local maximum'
    if D < 0:
        return 'saddle point'
    return 'inconclusive'

for p in crit:
    D, fxx = H.det().subs(p), H[0, 0].subs(p)
    print(p, ' D =', D, ' f_xx =', fxx, ':', classify(D, fxx), ' f =', f.subs(p))
Output
{x: 0, y: 0}  D = -9  f_xx = 0 : saddle point  f = 0
{x: 1, y: 1}  D = 27  f_xx = 6 : local minimum  f = -1

Without real=True, solve also returns the points where xxx is one of the two complex cube roots of 1 (the zeros of x2+x+1),x^2 + x + 1\mathclose{\text{),}}x2+x+1), which have no place on a map of the plane:

Python
u, v = sp.symbols('u v')                  # no assumptions
g = u**3 + v**3 - 3*u*v
print(len(sp.solve([sp.diff(g, u), sp.diff(g, v)], [u, v], dict=True)), 'solutions')
Output
4 solutions

Absolute extrema on closed bounded regions

Module 8 found the absolute extreme values of a continuous function on a closed interval [a,b][a, b][a,b] by comparing its values at the critical numbers and at the two endpoints. In two variables the interval becomes a region, and we must check its whole boundary, usually made of curves.

Definition 18.5Interior, boundary, closed and bounded

Let RRR be a set of points of the plane. A point PPP is an interior point of RRR if some open disc centred at PPP lies in R,R\mathclose{\text{,}}R, and a boundary point of RRR if every open disc centred at PPP contains points of RRR and points not in R.R\mathclose{\text{.}}R. The set RRR is closed if it contains all its boundary points, and bounded if it lies inside some disc.

The disc x2+y2≤1x^2 + y^2 \le 1x2+y2≤1 is closed and bounded; its boundary is the circle x2+y2=1.x^2 + y^2 = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}x2+y2=1. The open disc x2+y2<1x^2 + y^2 < 1x2+y2<1 is bounded but not closed, since it leaves out the whole circle. A rectangle with its sides, the set of points with a≤x≤ba \le x \le ba≤x≤b and c≤y≤d,c \le y \le d\mathclose{\text{,}}c≤y≤d, is closed and bounded, and so is a triangle with its sides. The half-plane y≥0y \ge 0y≥0 is closed but not bounded.

Theorem 18.3The Extreme Value Theorem in two variables

If fff is continuous on a nonempty, closed, bounded set RRR in the plane, then fff has an absolute maximum value f(x1,y1)f(x_1, y_1)f(x1​,y1​) and an absolute minimum value f(x2,y2)f(x_2, y_2)f(x2​,y2​) on R,R\mathclose{\text{,}}R, at some points (x1,y1)(x_1, y_1)(x1​,y1​) and (x2,y2)(x_2, y_2)(x2​,y2​) of R.R\mathclose{\text{.}}R.

As for the one-variable theorem of Module 3, the proof belongs to real analysis, and this series uses the theorem without proof; it holds in three or more variables too. Each hypothesis is needed. On the open disc x2+y2<1,x^2 + y^2 < 1\mathclose{\text{,}}x2+y2<1, f(x,y)=x+yf(x, y) = x + yf(x,y)=x+y has no maximum: its values come as close to 2\sqrt22​ as you like near (12,12),\big(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big)\mathclose{\text{,}}(2​1​,2​1​), a point of the missing circle, but never reach it. On the half-plane y≥0y \ge 0y≥0 the same fff is not bounded. And on the closed disc, the function equal to x+yx + yx+y except at (12,12),\big(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}, \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\big)\mathclose{\text{,}}(2​1​,2​1​), where it is 0, is not continuous and has no maximum.

Theorem 18.4Where the absolute extreme values are

Let fff be continuous on a nonempty, closed, bounded set R.R\mathclose{\text{.}}R. Then fff has an absolute maximum value and an absolute minimum value on R,R\mathclose{\text{,}}R, and each of them is taken at a boundary point of RRR or at a critical point of fff that is an interior point of R.R\mathclose{\text{.}}R.

Proof

By Theorem 18.3, the absolute maximum value on RRR is f(P)f(P)f(P) for some point PPP of R.R\mathclose{\text{.}}R. If PPP is a boundary point, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise PPP is an interior point: some open disc centred at PPP lies in R,R\mathclose{\text{,}}R, and f(P)≥ff(P) \ge ff(P)≥f on that disc, so f(P)f(P)f(P) is a local maximum value. If both partial derivatives exist at P,P\mathclose{\text{,}}P, they are 0 by Theorem 18.1; if not, PPP is a critical point by definition. The minimum is the same.

∎
Key idea

The closed region method. To find the absolute extreme values of a continuous function fff on a nonempty, closed, bounded region R:R\mathclose{\text{:}}R:

  1. Find the critical points of fff inside R,R\mathclose{\text{,}}R, and the values of fff there.
  2. Find the largest and the smallest values of fff on the boundary of R.R\mathclose{\text{.}}R. Usually the boundary consists of pieces (the sides of a polygon, arcs of curves) on each of which fff becomes a function of one variable: substitute the equation of a side, such as y=2,y = 2\mathclose{\text{,}}y=2, or a parametrisation, such as (cos⁡t,sin⁡t)(\cos t, \sin t)(cost,sint) on a circle, and use the closed interval method of Module 8, with the ends of each piece.
  3. The largest of all these values is the absolute maximum value; the smallest is the absolute minimum value.

As in one variable, no test of the critical points is needed: you compare a list of numbers.

Example 18.4The extreme values on a square✓ Checked

Find the absolute maximum and minimum values of f(x,y)=x3+y3−3xyf(x, y) = x^3 + y^3 - 3xyf(x,y)=x3+y3−3xy on the square RRR of points with −1≤x≤2-1 \le x \le 2−1≤x≤2 and −1≤y≤2.-1 \le y \le 2\mathclose{\text{.}}−1≤y≤2.

Lagrange multipliers

Many problems ask for the best point of a curve or a surface: the largest rectangle that fits in an ellipse, the point of a curve closest to a given point, the box with the most volume for a given amount of cardboard. Their variables are tied by an equation g(x,y)=c,g(x, y) = c\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x,y)=c, a constraint. Section 18.3 parametrised the boundary; that works when a parametrisation is easy to find. The method of this section works with the equation itself, and its picture explains every answer.

Take the largest rectangle, with sides parallel to the axes, inside the ellipse x24+y2=1.\tfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}4x2​+y2=1. We can centre it at the origin: moving any such rectangle there decreases or preserves the largest absolute xxx-coordinate and the largest absolute yyy-coordinate of its corners, so it still fits and has the same area. Then enlarge it until its corners reach the ellipse. Now the picture (Figure 18.3). For k>0,k > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}k>0, the level curves of the area, 4xy=k,4xy = k\mathclose{\text{,}}4xy=k, are hyperbolas. When 0<k<40 < k < 40<k<4 the level curve crosses the quarter of the ellipse twice: two rectangles in the ellipse have that area. As kkk grows towards 4, the two crossing points move together, and at k=4k = 4k=4 they merge: the level curve touches the ellipse. For k>4k > 4k>4 it misses the ellipse altogether. Where the two curves touch they have the same tangent line, so the vectors perpendicular to them are parallel. Theorem 18.5Lagrange multipliers

∎

The number λ\lambdaλ is a Lagrange multiplier. The same holds in three variables, with fff and ggg again having continuous first partial derivatives near the point: if f(x,y,z),f(x, y, z)\mathclose{\text{,}}f(x,y,z), restricted to the surface g(x,y,z)=c,g(x, y, z) = c\mathclose{\text{,}}g(x,y,z)=c, has a local extremum at a point where ∇g≠0,\nabla g \ne \vb{0}\mathclose{\text{,}}∇g=0, then ∇f=λ∇g\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g∇f=λ∇g there. The proof is the same, with the three-variable implicit function theorem, applied to every curve in the surface through the point: ∇f\nabla f∇f is perpendicular to all their tangent vectors, which fill the plane perpendicular to ∇g,\nabla g\mathclose{\text{,}}∇g, so ∇f\nabla f∇f is a multiple of ∇g.\nabla g\mathclose{\text{.}}∇g. The multiple can be 0: the theorem allows ∇f=0.\nabla f = \vb{0}\mathclose{\text{.}}∇f=0.

Key idea

The method of Lagrange multipliers. Suppose fff and ggg have continuous first partial derivatives near the constraint curve. To find the extreme values of f(x,y)f(x, y)f(x,y) subject to g(x,y)=c:g(x, y) = c\mathclose{\text{:}}g(x,y)=c:

  1. Solve the equations fx=λgx,f_x = \lambda g_x\mathclose{\text{,}}fx​=λgx​, fy=λgyf_y = \lambda g_yfy​=λgy​ and g(x,y)=cg(x, y) = cg(x,y)=c for x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, yyy and λ.\lambda\mathclose{\text{.}}λ.
  2. Add the points of the curve where ∇g=0,\nabla g = \vb{0}\mathclose{\text{,}}∇g=0, and the ends of the curve if it has ends.
  3. Evaluate fff at all these points. If the curve is nonempty, closed and bounded, like a circle or an ellipse, the largest value is the maximum and the smallest the minimum (Theorem 18.3). Otherwise an extra argument must show that an extremum exists.

In three variables, solve ∇f=λ∇g\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g∇f=λ∇g and g(x,y,z)=c:g(x, y, z) = c\mathclose{\text{:}}g(x,y,z)=c: four equations for x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, y,y\mathclose{\text{,}}y, zzz and λ.\lambda\mathclose{\text{.}}λ.

Going deeperWhat the multiplier measures

In the examples, λ\lambdaλ was found and then forgotten. It has a meaning. Let M(c)M(c)M(c) be the largest value of fff on the curve g=c,g = c\mathclose{\text{,}}g=c, taken at a point (x(c),y(c))\big(x(c), y(c)\big)(x(c),y(c)) with multiplier λ(c).\lambda(c)\mathclose{\text{.}}λ(c). Suppose that this family is defined for ccc in an open interval, that x(c)x(c)x(c) and y(c)y(c)y(c) are differentiable there, and that fff and ggg have continuous first partial derivatives near these points. Then

M′(c)=λ(c).M'(c) = \lambda(c).M′(c)=λ(c).

Indeed M(c)=f(x(c),y(c)),M(c) = f\big(x(c), y(c)\big)\mathclose{\text{,}}M(c)=f(x(c),y(c)), and by the chain rule and the Lagrange equations

M′(c)=fxx′+fyy′=λ (gxx′+gyy′)=λ ddc g(x(c),y(c))=λ ddc c=λ.\begin{aligned} M'(c) &= f_x x' + f_y y' = \lambda\,(g_x x' + g_y y') \\ &= \lambda\,\frac{d}{dc}\,g\big(x(c), y(c)\big) = \lambda\,\frac{d}{dc}\,c = \lambda. \end{aligned}M′(c)​=fx​x′+fy​y′=λ(gx​x′+gy​y′)=λdcd​g(x(c),y(c))=λdcd​c=λ.​

The same argument works for the smallest value. So λ\lambdaλ is the rate at which the best value changes as the constraint level changes: if ccc is a budget, λ\lambdaλ is about what one more unit of budget is worth at the optimum, provided that unit is small enough for the linear approximation. Economists call it a shadow price.

For the rectangle in the ellipse x24+y2=c\tfrac{x^2}{4} + y^2 = c4x2​+y2=c with c>0,c > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}c>0, the steps of Example 18.5 give the corner (2c,c/2)\big(\sqrt{2c}, \sqrt{c/2}\big)(2c​,c/2​) and the largest area M(c)=4c,M(c) = 4c\mathclose{\text{,}}M(c)=4c, so M′(c)=4:M'(c) = 4\mathclose{\text{:}}M′(c)=4: the λ=4\lambda = 4λ=4 found there. For the box with AAA cm² of cardboard, where A>0,A > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}A>0, they give x=y=2zx = y = 2zx=y=2z with 12z2=A,12z^2 = A\mathclose{\text{,}}12z2=A, so the largest volume is V(A)=4z3=4(A12)3/2,V(A) = 4z^3 = 4\big(\tfrac{A}{12}\big)^{3/2}\mathclose{\text{,}}V(A)=4z3=4(12A​)3/2, and V′(A)=12(A12)1/2=z2,V'(A) = \tfrac12\big(\tfrac{A}{12}\big)^{1/2} = \tfrac{z}{2}\mathclose{\text{,}}V′(A)=21​(12A​)1/2=2z​, which at A=300A = 300A=300 is 52:\tfrac52\mathclose{\text{:}}25​: the multiplier of Example 18.7. Each extra cm² of cardboard adds about 2.5 cm³ of volume, near this size.

Two constraints

Suppose that f,f\mathclose{\text{,}}f, ggg and hhh have continuous first partial derivatives near a point where g(x,y,z)=cg(x, y, z) = cg(x,y,z)=c and h(x,y,z)=d.h(x, y, z) = d\mathclose{\text{.}}h(x,y,z)=d. To find extreme values of fff on their intersection, add a second multiplier μ,\mu\mathclose{\text{,}}μ, read “mu”: at a constrained local extremum,

∇f=λ ∇g+μ ∇h,\nabla f = \lambda\,\nabla g + \mu\,\nabla h,∇f=λ∇g+μ∇h,

provided ∇g\nabla g∇g and ∇h\nabla h∇h are not parallel there (and neither is 0).\vb{0}\mathclose{\text{).}}0). These hypotheses ensure that the intersection is locally a differentiable curve with a nonzero tangent vector, by a version of the implicit function theorem of Module 17. The reason for the multiplier equation is the same as before. The curve lies in both surfaces, so its tangent vector T\vb{T}T is perpendicular to ∇g\nabla g∇g and to ∇h;\nabla h\mathclose{\text{;}}∇h; and at an extremum ∇f\nabla f∇f is perpendicular to T\vb{T}T too. The vectors perpendicular to T\vb{T}T form a plane, and two non-parallel vectors in it, ∇g\nabla g∇g and ∇h,\nabla h\mathclose{\text{,}}∇h, combine to give every vector of the plane, ∇f\nabla f∇f included. With the two constraints, that makes five equations for x,x\mathclose{\text{,}}x, y,y\mathclose{\text{,}}y, z,z\mathclose{\text{,}}z, λ\lambdaλ and μ.\mu\mathclose{\text{.}}μ.

Example 18.8The highest point of a tilted circle✓ Checked

The plane x+y+z=0x + y + z = 0x+y+z=0 meets the sphere x2+y2+z2=6x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 6x2+y2+z2=6 in a circle. Find its highest and lowest points.

Maximise and minimise f=zf = zf=z subject to g=x+y+z=0g = x + y + z = 0g=x+y+z=0 and h=x2+y2+z2=6.h = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 = 6\mathclose{\text{.}}h=x2+y2+z2=6. 0=λ+2μx,0=λ+2μy,1=λ+2μz,\begin{aligned} 0 &= \lambda + 2\mu x, \\ 0 &= \lambda + 2\mu y, \\ 1 &= \lambda + 2\mu z, \end{aligned}001​=λ+2μx,=λ+2μy,=λ+2μz,​

with the two constraints. Subtracting the first two gives 2μ(x−y)=0.2\mu(x - y) = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}2μ(x−y)=0. If μ=0,\mu = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}μ=0, the first gives λ=0,\lambda = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}λ=0, and then the third says 1=0,1 = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}1=0, which is impossible; so x=y.x = y\mathclose{\text{.}}x=y. The plane then gives z=−2x,z = -2x\mathclose{\text{,}}z=−2x, and the sphere x2+x2+4x2=6,x^2 + x^2 + 4x^2 = 6\mathclose{\text{,}}x2+x2+4x2=6, so x=±1.x = \pm1\mathclose{\text{.}}x=±1. The gradients ⟨1,1,1⟩\langle 1, 1, 1\rangle⟨1,1,1⟩ and ⟨2x,2y,2z⟩\langle 2x, 2y, 2z\rangle⟨2x,2y,2z⟩ are parallel only where x=y=z,x = y = z\mathclose{\text{,}}x=y=z, which on the plane means the origin, not on the sphere; so the method applies everywhere on the circle. The circle is closed and bounded, so fff has a largest and a smallest value on it (the Extreme Value Theorem in three variables), and they are among the candidates: the highest point is (−1,−1,2)(-1, -1, 2)(−1,−1,2) and the lowest is (1,1,−2).(1, 1, -2)\mathclose{\text{.}}(1,1,−2).

Compute itLagrange systems with SymPy

solve handles the systems of this section. Declaring the dimensions positive keeps only the boxes that can be built; the multiplier is left real:

Python
import sympy as sp
x, y, z = sp.symbols('x y z', positive=True)
lam = sp.symbols('lambda', real=True)
V = x*y*z                                   # the open box of Example 18.7
g = x*y + 2*x*z + 2*y*z
eqs = [sp.diff(V, s) - lam*sp.diff(g, s) for s in (x, y, z)] + [g - 300]
print(sp.solve(eqs, [x, y, z, lam], dict=True))
Output
[{lambda: 5/2, x: 10, y: 10, z: 5}]

With two constraints there are two multipliers; here the unknowns are real, of either sign:

Python
x, y, z, lam, mu = sp.symbols('x y z lambda mu', real=True)
f, g, h = z, x + y + z, x**2 + y**2 + z**2   # Example 18.8
eqs = [sp.diff(f, s) - lam*sp.diff(g, s) - mu*sp.diff(h, s) for s in (x, y, z)]
eqs += [g, h - 6]
for sol in sp.solve(eqs, [x, y, z, lam, mu], dict=True):
    print(sol, ' f =', f.subs(sol))
Output
{lambda: 1/3, mu: -1/6, x: 1, y: 1, z: -2}  f = -2
{lambda: 1/3, mu: 1/6, x: -1, y: -1, z: 2}  f = 2

solve finds the candidates; deciding which is the maximum, and whether a maximum exists, is still your job.

5

Least squares

Data from an experiment or a log file often lie roughly along a line, and you want the line that fits them best. Suppose, hypothetically, that five measurements give the points (0,1),(0, 1)\mathclose{\text{,}}(0,1), (1,4),(1, 4)\mathclose{\text{,}}(1,4), (2,3),(2, 3)\mathclose{\text{,}}(2,3), (3,6)(3, 6)(3,6) and (4,6)(4, 6)(4,6) (made-up numbers). No line passes through all five. For a line y=mx+b,y = mx + b\mathclose{\text{,}}y=mx+b, the residual, or error, of the point (xi,yi)(x_i, y_i)(xi​,yi​) is

ei=yi−(mxi+b),e_i = y_i - (mx_i + b),ei​=yi​−(mxi​+b),

the vertical distance, with a sign, from the line up to the point. One number measures how badly the line misses all the points at once: the sum of squared errors

E(m,b)=∑i=1n(yi−mxi−b)2.E(m, b) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\big(y_i - mx_i - b\big)^2.E(m,b)=i=1∑n​(yi​−mxi​−b)2.

Here the data are fixed numbers, and the unknowns are the slope mmm and the intercept b:b\mathclose{\text{:}}b: EEE is a function of two variables.

Definition 18.6Least-squares line

A least-squares line, or regression line, of a nonempty finite collection of data points (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)(x1​,y1​),…,(xn​,yn​) is a line y=mx+by = mx + by=mx+b whose slope and intercept minimise the sum of squared errors E(m,b).E(m, b)\mathclose{\text{.}}E(m,b). The next theorem gives the condition for this line to be unique.

Squares, rather than absolute values of the errors, make EEE a smooth function of mmm and b,b\mathclose{\text{,}}b, so that calculus applies; a large error can outweigh several smaller ones, which matters when the data contain a wild value. Mathematical Foundations’ least squares module treats the same problem with vectors and projections; here partial derivatives find the answer.

Theorem 18.6The normal equations

Let (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)(x1​,y1​),…,(xn​,yn​) be data points with at least two different xi.x_i\mathclose{\text{.}}xi​. Then E(m,b)E(m, b)E(m,b) has exactly one critical point, the solution of the normal equations

(∑xi2)m+(∑xi)b=∑xiyi,(∑xi)m+nb=∑yi,\begin{aligned} \Big(\sum x_i^2\Big)m + \Big(\sum x_i\Big)b &= \sum x_iy_i, \\ \Big(\sum x_i\Big)m + nb &= \sum y_i, \end{aligned}(∑xi2​)m+(∑xi​)b(∑xi​)m+nb​=∑xi​yi​,=∑yi​,​

and EEE takes its absolute minimum value there, and nowhere else. (Each sum runs over i=1,…,n.)i = 1, \dots, n\mathclose{\text{.)}}i=1,…,n.)

Proof

The critical point. EEE is a polynomial in mmm and b.b\mathclose{\text{.}}b. By the chain rule,

∂E∂m=−2∑xi(yi−mxi−b),∂E∂b=−2∑(yi−mxi−b).\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial E}{\partial m} &= -2\sum x_i\big(y_i - mx_i - b\big), \\ \frac{\partial E}{\partial b} &= -2\sum\big(y_i - mx_i - b\big). \end{aligned}∂m∂E​∂b∂E​​=−2∑xi​(yi​−mxi​−b),=−2∑(yi​−mxi​−b).​

Setting both to 0 and moving the terms with mmm and bbb to the left gives the normal equations. To solve them, let xˉ=1n∑xi\bar x = \tfrac1n\sum x_ixˉ=n1​∑xi​ and yˉ=1n∑yi\bar y = \tfrac1n\sum y_iyˉ​=n1​∑yi​ be the means, read “x bar” and “y bar”. The second equation divided by nnn says b=yˉ−mxˉ.b = \bar y - m\bar x\mathclose{\text{.}}b=yˉ​−mxˉ. Substituting this into the first gives

(∑xi2−nxˉ2)m=∑xiyi−nxˉyˉ.\Big(\sum x_i^2 - n\bar x^2\Big)m = \sum x_iy_i - n\bar x\bar y.(∑xi2​−nxˉ2)m=∑xi​yi​−nxˉyˉ​.

Expanding the square shows that ∑(xi−xˉ)2=∑xi2−2xˉ∑xi+nxˉ2=∑xi2−nxˉ2,\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 = \sum x_i^2 - 2\bar x\sum x_i + n\bar x^2 = \sum x_i^2 - n\bar x^2\mathclose{\text{,}}∑(xi​−xˉ)2=∑xi2​−2xˉ∑xi​+nxˉ2=∑xi2​−nxˉ2, and this is positive, because not every xix_ixi​ equals xˉ.\bar x\mathclose{\text{.}}xˉ. So mmm is determined, then b:b\mathclose{\text{:}}b: exactly one solution (m∗,b∗).(m^*, b^*)\mathclose{\text{.}}(m∗,b∗).

The minimum. Let ei=yi−m∗xi−b∗e_i = y_i - m^*x_i - b^*ei​=yi​−m∗xi​−b∗ be the residuals of this line. The normal equations say exactly that ∑ei=0\sum e_i = 0∑ei​=0 and ∑xiei=0.\sum x_ie_i = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}∑xi​ei​=0. For any other line, with m=m∗+pm = m^* + pm=m∗+p and b=b∗+q,b = b^* + q\mathclose{\text{,}}b=b∗+q,

E(m∗+p,b∗+q)=∑(ei−pxi−q)2=∑ei2−2p∑xiei−2q∑ei+∑(pxi+q)2=E(m∗,b∗)+∑(pxi+q)2.\begin{aligned} &E(m^* + p, b^* + q) \\ &\quad= \sum\big(e_i - px_i - q\big)^2 \\ &\quad= \sum e_i^2 - 2p\sum x_ie_i - 2q\sum e_i \\ &\qquad + \sum\big(px_i + q\big)^2 \\ &\quad= E(m^*, b^*) + \sum\big(px_i + q\big)^2. \end{aligned}​E(m∗+p,b∗+q)=∑(ei​−pxi​−q)2=∑ei2​−2p∑xi​ei​−2q∑ei​+∑(pxi​+q)2=E(m∗,b∗)+∑(pxi​+q)2.​

The last sum is never negative, and it is 0 only when pxi+q=0px_i + q = 0pxi​+q=0 for every i;i\mathclose{\text{;}}i; for two different xix_ixi​ that forces p=q=0.p = q = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}p=q=0.

∎

So the least-squares line passes through the mean point (xˉ,yˉ),(\bar x, \bar y)\mathclose{\text{,}}(xˉ,yˉ​), and its slope is

m=∑xiyi−nxˉyˉ∑xi2−nxˉ2.m = \frac{\sum x_iy_i - n\bar x\bar y}{\sum x_i^2 - n\bar x^2}.m=∑xi2​−nxˉ2∑xi​yi​−nxˉyˉ​​.
Example 18.9Fitting a line to five points✓ Checked

Find the least-squares line of the points (0,1),(0, 1)\mathclose{\text{,}}(0,1), (1,4),(1, 4)\mathclose{\text{,}}(1,4), (2,3),(2, 3)\mathclose{\text{,}}(2,3), (3,6)(3, 6)(3,6) and (4,6),(4, 6)\mathclose{\text{,}}(4,6), its residuals and E.E\mathclose{\text{.}}E.

The sums: n=5,n = 5\mathclose{\text{,}}n=5, ∑xi=10,\sum x_i = 10\mathclose{\text{,}}∑xi​=10, ∑xi2=0+1+4+9+16=30,\sum x_i^2 = 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30\mathclose{\text{,}}∑xi2​=0+1+4+9+16=30, ∑yi=20\sum y_i = 20∑yi​=20 and ∑xiyi=0+4+6+18+24=52.\sum x_iy_i = 0 + 4 + 6 + 18 + 24 = 52\mathclose{\text{.}}∑xi​yi​=0+4+6+18+24=52. E(1.2,1.6)=0.36+1.44+1.00+0.64+0.16=3.6,E(1.2, 1.6) = 0.36 + 1.44 + 1.00 + 0.64 + 0.16 = 3.6,E(1.2,1.6)=0.36+1.44+1.00+0.64+0.16=3.6,

Compute itLeast squares with NumPy

The normal equations are two linear equations for mmm and b,b\mathclose{\text{,}}b, and np.linalg.solve solves them. NumPy also has a ready-made fit, np.polyfit:

Python
import numpy as np
xs = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4])
ys = np.array([1, 4, 3, 6, 6])
n = len(xs)
A = np.array([[np.sum(xs**2), np.sum(xs)],
              [np.sum(xs),    n]])
rhs = np.array([np.sum(xs*ys), np.sum(ys)])
m, b = np.linalg.solve(A, rhs)               # the normal equations
print(f"normal equations: m = {m:.4f}, b = {b:.4f}")
print("np.polyfit:", np.polyfit(xs, ys, 1))
e = ys - (m*xs + b)
print("residuals:", np.round(e, 4), " E =", round(float(np.sum(e**2)), 4))
Output
normal equations: m = 1.2000, b = 1.6000
np.polyfit: [1.2 1.6]
residuals: [-0.6  1.2 -1.   0.8 -0.4]  E = 3.6

np.polyfit(xs, ys, 1) fits a polynomial of degree 1 and returns its coefficients highest power first, [m,b],[m, b]\mathclose{\text{,}}[m,b], here as floating-point numbers. With degree 2 it fits y=ax2+bx+cy = ax^2 + bx + cy=ax2+bx+c by least squares; the minimiser satisfies three normal equations and is unique when there are at least three distinct input values. The fitted coefficient aaa can be 0, so the result need not be a parabola. The numerical routine solves a scaled least-squares system rather than forming these normal equations. NumPy recommends numpy.polynomial.Polynomial.fit for new code because it is more stable numerically.

Watch out

Three slips with least squares. Expecting the line to treat xxx and yyy alike: it minimises vertical errors. Fitting xxx as a function of yyy to the data of Example 18.9 gives x=23y−23,x = \tfrac23y - \tfrac23\mathclose{\text{,}}x=32​y−32​, that is, y=1.5x+1,y = 1.5x + 1\mathclose{\text{,}}y=1.5x+1, a different line (both pass through the mean point). Forgetting the condition: if every xix_ixi​ equals the same number a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, only the fitted value ma+bma + bma+b is determined. It must equal yˉ,\bar y\mathclose{\text{,}}yˉ​, so infinitely many pairs with b=yˉ−mab = \bar y - mab=yˉ​−ma minimise E.E\mathclose{\text{.}}E. Trusting a fit blindly: a least-squares fit exists for every nonempty finite data set, even data that follow a curve. A pattern in the residuals, such as positive at both ends and negative in the middle, suggests that a line is a poor model; it is evidence, not proof, because measurements can contain noise.

6

Gradient descent: step size and conditioning

Solving ∇f=0\nabla f = \vb{0}∇f=0 by algebra works only for simple functions. A machine-learning model may have millions of parameters, and training often seeks smaller loss by gradient descent, met in one variable in Module 8 and in two in Module 17. For a differentiable function f,f\mathclose{\text{,}}f, from a starting point x0,\vb{x}_0\mathclose{\text{,}}x0​, with a step size η>0\eta > 0η>0 (“eta”),

xk+1=xk−η ∇f(xk),k=0,1,2,…,\vb{x}_{k+1} = \vb{x}_k - \eta\,\nabla f(\vb{x}_k), \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \dots,xk+1​=xk​−η∇f(xk​),k=0,1,2,…,

where xk=⟨xk,yk⟩,\vb{x}_k = \langle x_k, y_k\rangle\mathclose{\text{,}}xk​=⟨xk​,yk​⟩, and each new point must stay in the domain. A nonzero gradient gives the direction of fastest decrease through −∇f,-\nabla f\mathclose{\text{,}}−∇f, but a finite step can still increase fff if it is too large. Example 8.18 showed that on the parabola q2x2,\tfrac q2x^2\mathclose{\text{,}}2q​x2, with q>0,q > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}q>0, convergence to the minimum from every starting point holds exactly when 0<η<2/q.0 < \eta < 2/q\mathclose{\text{.}}0<η<2/q. In two variables a bowl can curve more steeply in one direction than in another, and that affects the choice of step size.

The two coordinates evolve separately: xk=−6(0.82)kx_k = -6(0.82)^kxk​=−6(0.82)k and yk=2.5(−0.8)k.y_k = 2.5(-0.8)^k\mathclose{\text{.}}yk​=2.5(−0.8)k. The table shows the points and the values of fff there:

Theorem 18.7Gradient descent on a quadratic bowl

Let f(x,y)=12(ax2+cy2)f(x, y) = \tfrac12(ax^2 + cy^2)f(x,y)=21​(ax2+cy2) with 0<a≤c.0 < a \le c\mathclose{\text{.}}0<a≤c. Proof

∇f=⟨ax,cy⟩,\nabla f = \langle ax, cy\rangle\mathclose{\text{,}}∇f=⟨ax,cy⟩, so xk+1=(1−ηa)xkx_{k+1} = (1 - \eta a)x_kxk+1​=(1−ηa)xk​ and yk+1=(1−ηc)yk,y_{k+1} = (1 - \eta c)y_k\mathclose{\text{,}}yk+1​=(1−ηc)yk​, and therefore xk=(1−ηa)kx0x_k = (1 - \eta a)^kx_0xk​=(1−ηa)kx0​ and yk=(1−ηc)ky0.y_k = (1 - \eta c)^ky_0\mathclose{\text{.}}yk​=(1−ηc)ky0​. As in Example 8.18, the powers rkr^krk of a number rrr tend to 0 exactly when ∣r∣<1.\abs{r} < 1\mathclose{\text{.}}∣r∣<1. To converge from every start, including starts with x0≠0x_0 \ne 0x0​=0 and y0≠0,y_0 \ne 0\mathclose{\text{,}}y0​=0, gradient descent needs ∣1−ηa∣<1\abs{1 - \eta a} < 1∣1−ηa∣<1 and ∣1−ηc∣<1,\abs{1 - \eta c} < 1\mathclose{\text{,}}∣1−ηc∣<1, that is, 0<η<2/a0 < \eta < 2/a0<η<2/a and 0<η<2/c.0 < \eta < 2/c\mathclose{\text{.}}0<η<2/c. Since a≤c,a \le c\mathclose{\text{,}}a≤c, 2/c≤2/a,2/c \le 2/a\mathclose{\text{,}}2/c≤2/a, and the two conditions together say 0<η<2/c.0 < \eta < 2/c\mathclose{\text{.}}0<η<2/c.

Ill-conditioning

Theorem 18.7 says that convergence from every starting point requires η<2/c,\eta < 2/c\mathclose{\text{,}}η<2/c, where ccc is the larger curvature. In the flatter direction, with curvature a,a\mathclose{\text{,}}a, the factor 1−ηa1 - \eta a1−ηa is then more than 1−2a/c,1 - 2a/c\mathclose{\text{,}}1−2a/c, which is close to 1 when ccc is much larger than a:a\mathclose{\text{:}}a: a nonzero coordinate in that direction creeps towards 0. To minimise the larger of the two coordinate factors in magnitude, the best fixed step is η∗=2a+c,\eta^* = \dfrac{2}{a + c}\mathclose{\text{,}}η∗=a+c2​, which makes the two factors equal in size:

1−η∗a=c−ac+a,1−η∗c=−c−ac+a.1 - \eta^*a = \frac{c - a}{c + a}, \qquad 1 - \eta^*c = -\frac{c - a}{c + a}.1−η∗a=c+ac−a​,1−η∗c=−c+ac−a​.

Exercise 18.10 shows that no other fixed step size makes that larger factor smaller. With κ=c/a,\kappa = c/a\mathclose{\text{,}}κ=c/a, read “kappa”, the condition number of the bowl, the factor is

c−ac+a=κ−1κ+1.\frac{c - a}{c + a} = \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}.c+ac−a​=κ+1κ−1​.

For the valley of Example 18.10, κ=10:\kappa = 10\mathclose{\text{:}}κ=10: this best fixed step is η∗=211≈0.18,\eta^* = \tfrac{2}{11} \approx 0.18\mathclose{\text{,}}η∗=112​≈0.18, and with it each step shrinks both coordinates, in size, by the factor 911≈0.82.\tfrac{9}{11} \approx 0.82\mathclose{\text{.}}119​≈0.82. When κ\kappaκ is large the factor is close to 1, and gradient descent is slow: to reduce the distance from the minimum by a fixed factor, the number of steps with η∗\eta^*η∗ grows asymptotically in proportion to κ\kappaκ (the Compute it box below counts them, and Exercise 18.10 explains why).

The picture explains it. For C>0,C > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}C>0, the level curves 12(ax2+cy2)=C\tfrac12(ax^2 + cy^2) = C21​(ax2+cy2)=C are ellipses with semi-axes 2C/a\sqrt{2C/a}2C/a​ and 2C/c,\sqrt{2C/c}\mathclose{\text{,}}2C/c​, so they are κ\sqrt\kappaκ​ times as long as they are wide. The gradient is perpendicular to the level curve through the point (Module 17), and often points across the valley rather than directly towards the minimum. A quadratic bowl with a large condition number, and hence long, thin elliptical level curves, is ill-conditioned. Gradient descent can zigzag on it, as in Figure 18.5, though smaller steps or a start on an axis need not zigzag.

Rescaling

The shape of the level curves depends on the variables you choose. Put v=10 yv = \sqrt{10}\,yv=10​y in Example 18.10: then f=12(x2+v2),f = \tfrac12(x^2 + v^2)\mathclose{\text{,}}f=21​(x2+v2), whose level curves in the (x,v)(x, v)(x,v) plane are circles, with κ=1.\kappa = 1\mathclose{\text{.}}κ=1. Its gradient is ⟨x,v⟩,\langle x, v\rangle\mathclose{\text{,}}⟨x,v⟩, which points straight away from the minimum, and gradient descent in xxx and vvv with η=1\eta = 1η=1 gives (x,v)−⟨x,v⟩=(0,0):(x, v) - \langle x, v\rangle = (0, 0)\mathclose{\text{:}}(x,v)−⟨x,v⟩=(0,0): the minimum in one step (Figure 18.5, right). In terms of the original variables, the new method divides each partial derivative by the curvature in its direction before stepping.

A common cause of ill-conditioning is variables measured on very different scales. One common preprocessing step is to standardise nonconstant input features: subtract each feature’s training-data mean and divide by its standard deviation, the square root of the mean squared distance from that mean. The transformed training values then have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. This can help conditioning, though it does not remove every cause, such as strongly related features. Even centring alone can help. For the data of Example 18.9, the second partial derivatives of E(m,b)E(m, b)E(m,b) are Emm=2∑xi2=60,E_{mm} = 2\sum x_i^2 = 60\mathclose{\text{,}}Emm​=2∑xi2​=60, Emb=2∑xi=20E_{mb} = 2\sum x_i = 20Emb​=2∑xi​=20 and Ebb=2n=10;E_{bb} = 2n = 10\mathclose{\text{;}}Ebb​=2n=10; the mixed term tilts the elliptical level curves, and they are long and thin. Centre the inputs, using xi−2x_i - 2xi​−2 in place of xi,x_i\mathclose{\text{,}}xi​, where 2 is their mean: then ∑(xi−2)=0,\sum (x_i - 2) = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}∑(xi​−2)=0, the mixed term disappears, and Emm=20,E_{mm} = 20\mathclose{\text{,}}Emm​=20, Emb=0,E_{mb} = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}Emb​=0, Ebb=10,E_{bb} = 10\mathclose{\text{,}}Ebb​=10, a condition number of 2. The fitted line is the same, y=1.2(x−2)+4=1.2x+1.6y = 1.2(x - 2) + 4 = 1.2x + 1.6y=1.2(x−2)+4=1.2x+1.6 (Exercise 18.12), but gradient descent finds it far faster in the computation below.

For a quadratic bowl whose elliptical level curves are tilted, the same analysis holds along the axes of the ellipses; their curvatures are the positive eigenvalues of the Hessian matrix, which Mathematical Foundations’ Module 13 studies. For a function with continuous second partial derivatives near a minimum, this gives a local guide when both Hessian eigenvalues there are positive: the quadratic approximation is a bowl. It is not a global convergence guarantee. A minimum with a zero eigenvalue, such as the origin for x4+y4,x^4 + y^4\mathclose{\text{,}}x4+y4, needs a different analysis. Mathematical Foundations’ Module 19 treats gradient methods and conditioning from the computing side, and the AI series shows them training real models.

Compute itCondition number and steps

How many steps does gradient descent with the best fixed step need on f=12(x2+κy2),f = \tfrac12(x^2 + \kappa y^2)\mathclose{\text{,}}f=21​(x2+κy2), from (1,1),(1, 1)\mathclose{\text{,}}(1,1), to bring the point a million times closer to the minimum?

Python
import math

def steps_needed(kappa, max_steps=100000):
    if not math.isfinite(kappa) or kappa < 1:
        raise ValueError("kappa must be finite and at least 1")
    eta = 2/(1 + kappa)                         # the best fixed step
    x, y = 1.0, 1.0
    for k in range(max_steps + 1):
        if math.hypot(x, y) <= 1e-6*math.sqrt(2):
            return k                           # completed updates
        if k == max_steps:
            break
        x, y = x - eta*x, y - eta*kappa*y
    raise RuntimeError("distance tolerance not reached within the step limit")

for kappa in (1, 10, 100, 1000):
    print(f"kappa = {kappa:4}   steps needed: {steps_needed(kappa)}")
Output
kappa =    1   steps needed: 1
kappa =   10   steps needed: 69
kappa =  100   steps needed: 691
kappa = 1000   steps needed: 6908

From κ=10\kappa = 10κ=10 onwards, each tenfold increase in this table multiplies the work by about ten. The step limit prevents an endless loop if the requested reduction takes too long or floating-point arithmetic stops making progress.

Now least squares: fit the line of Example 18.9 by gradient descent on E(m,b),E(m, b)\mathclose{\text{,}}E(m,b), with the raw inputs and with the inputs centred, using the same step size η=0.025\eta = 0.025η=0.025 for both, and stop when both partial derivatives have magnitude below 10−6:10^{-6}\mathclose{\text{:}}10−6:

Python
import numpy as np
xs = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3, 4.0])
ys = np.array([1, 4, 3, 6, 6.0])

def fit_by_descent(xs, ys, eta=0.025, max_steps=100000):
    m = b = 0.0
    for k in range(max_steps + 1):
        e = ys - (m*xs + b)                       # the residuals
        Em, Eb = -2*np.sum(xs*e), -2*np.sum(e)    # the partial derivatives of E
        if not np.isfinite([Em, Eb]).all():
            raise RuntimeError("nonfinite gradient; try a smaller step")
        if max(abs(Em), abs(Eb)) < 1e-6:
            return k, m, b                       # completed updates
        if k == max_steps:
            break
        m, b = m - eta*Em, b - eta*Eb
    raise RuntimeError("gradient tolerance not reached within the step limit")

for name, x in (("raw", xs), ("centred", xs - 2)):
    k, m, b = fit_by_descent(x, ys)
    print(f"{name:8} inputs: {k} steps, m = {m:.6f}, b = {b:.6f}")
Output
raw      inputs: 193 steps, m = 1.200000, b = 1.600000
centred  inputs: 61 steps, m = 1.200000, b = 4.000000

With the same step size, the centred inputs need 61 steps instead of 193. They also allow larger steps: the centred Hessian is diagonal with curvatures 20 and 10, so Theorem 18.7, applied after shifting the minimum to the origin, gives convergence from every start when 0<η<0.1.0 < \eta < 0.1\mathclose{\text{.}}0<η<0.1. From the same zero start, the raw inputs diverge already for η=0.03.\eta = 0.03\mathclose{\text{.}}η=0.03. The centred fit reports b≈4,b \approx 4\mathclose{\text{,}}b≈4, the intercept at x=2:x = 2\mathclose{\text{:}}x=2: the line y=1.2(x−2)+4,y = 1.2(x - 2) + 4\mathclose{\text{,}}y=1.2(x−2)+4, the same line as before. Both functions report an error if their tolerance is not reached within the permitted number of updates.

Watch out

Three slips with gradient descent. “A larger step is always faster”: a larger step can be worse even below 2/c.2/c\mathclose{\text{.}}2/c. For the quadratic bowl, a step above 2/c2/c2/c makes any nonzero component in the steepest direction grow. “Gradient descent heads for the minimum”: a nonzero negative gradient gives the direction of steepest local decrease. On an elliptical bowl it points directly at the minimum on the axes, but usually across the valley elsewhere; circular level curves make every such direction radial. “It always finds a minimum”: it need not converge, and even a convergent sequence can reach a saddle. On f=x2−y2,f = x^2 - y^2\mathclose{\text{,}}f=x2−y2, with 0<η<1,0 < \eta < 1\mathclose{\text{,}}0<η<1, a start on the xxx-axis stays there and converges to the saddle at the origin; a start off the axis escapes because its yyy-coordinate is multiplied by 1+2η>11 + 2\eta > 11+2η>1 at every step.

What you learned

  • A local extremum of f(x,y)f(x, y)f(x,y) is at a critical point, where ∇f=0\nabla f = \vb{0}∇f=0 or a partial derivative does not exist. An interior critical point that is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum is a saddle point, like the origin for x2−y2.x^2 - y^2\mathclose{\text{.}}x2−y2.
  • The second derivative test applies at an interior point where ∇f=0,\nabla f = \vb{0}\mathclose{\text{,}}∇f=0, when the second partial derivatives are continuous nearby. With D=fxxfyy−fxy2,D = f_{xx}f_{yy} - f_{xy}^2\mathclose{\text{,}}D=fxx​fyy​−fxy2​, the determinant of the Hessian matrix: D>0D > 0D>0 and fxx>0,f_{xx} > 0\mathclose{\text{,}}fxx​>0, local minimum; D>0D > 0D>0 and fxx<0,f_{xx} < 0\mathclose{\text{,}}fxx​<0, local maximum; D<0,D < 0\mathclose{\text{,}}D<0, saddle point; D=0,D = 0\mathclose{\text{,}}D=0, inconclusive. It reads the sign of the quadratic approximation.
  • A continuous function on a nonempty, closed, bounded region has absolute extreme values (the Extreme Value Theorem): compare its values at the critical points inside with its extreme values on the boundary, found piece by piece with one-variable methods.
  • Lagrange multipliers: for fff and ggg with continuous first partial derivatives nearby, an extremum of fff on g=cg = cg=c where ∇g≠0\nabla g \ne \vb{0}∇g=0 satisfies ∇f=λ∇g.\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g\mathclose{\text{.}}∇f=λ∇g. Add singular points and any ends of the constraint, compare, and make sure an extremum exists. With two such constraints and independent gradients, ∇f=λ∇g+μ∇h.\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g + \mu\nabla h\mathclose{\text{.}}∇f=λ∇g+μ∇h. Along a differentiable family of optimal points, the multiplier is the rate at which the best value changes with c.c\mathclose{\text{.}}c.
  • Least squares: the line y=mx+by = mx + by=mx+b that minimises E(m,b)=∑(yi−mxi−b)2E(m, b) = \sum(y_i - mx_i - b)^2E(m,b)=∑(yi​−mxi​−b)2 solves the normal equations, ∂E/∂m=∂E/∂b=0.\partial E/\partial m = \partial E/\partial b = 0\mathclose{\text{.}}∂E/∂m=∂E/∂b=0. It passes through the mean point and is unique when at least two inputs differ.
  • Gradient descent on a bowl 12(ax2+cy2),\tfrac12(ax^2 + cy^2)\mathclose{\text{,}}21​(ax2+cy2), with 0<a≤c,0 < a \le c\mathclose{\text{,}}0<a≤c, converges from every starting point exactly when 0<η<2/c.0 < \eta < 2/c\mathclose{\text{.}}0<η<2/c. The best fixed step shrinks the distance to the minimum by κ−1κ+1\tfrac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}κ+1κ−1​ per step, where κ=c/a\kappa = c/aκ=c/a is the condition number. Long, thin level curves can lead to slow, zigzagging paths; rescaling or centring can help.
